questions.q: This lesson combines four earlier lessons into one self-review pass. Which four, in order?
options: Comparison (Lesson 6), failure-mode checklist (Lesson 7), security checklist (Lesson 8), ADR documentation (Lesson 9)
The five case studies from Chapter 1, run in numerical order
Only the security checklist and the ADR format -- comparison and failure modes aren't part of the pass
Presenting (Lesson 11), objections (Lesson 12), wrap-up (Lesson 13), mock review (Lesson 14)
questions.explain: The self-review pass runs Lesson 6's comparison method, Lesson 7's failure-mode checklist, and Lesson 8's security checklist, and then captures the results using Lesson 9's ADR format -- four distinct tools used together in sequence.

questions.q: What specific discipline does this lesson say self-review requires that a simple reread doesn't?
options: Reading the design out loud to a colleague
Deliberately answering each step honestly, especially the step that would be awkward to answer honestly, rather than unconsciously picking weak alternatives or softening gaps
Running the design through an automated linter
Waiting at least one week before reviewing your own design
questions.explain: The lesson specifically warns against unconsciously softening the hardest parts -- picking a weak alternative, skimming a real failure gap, or answering security questions with the intended design rather than the documented one. The step that's awkward to answer honestly is exactly the one that most needs it.

questions.q: In the Vantage Utilities worked example, what gap did step 2 (failure modes) surface that Lesson 4's original write-up had missed?
options: That the portal does not use Salesforce at all
That out-of-order delivery had been named but never actually given a concrete fix -- only acknowledged, not solved
That authentication had never been considered for this case study
That Lesson 4 used too many Key Terms
questions.explain: The worked example shows out-of-order delivery was flagged in Lesson 7 but left as an acknowledged risk rather than a solved one in Lesson 4's original design -- exactly the kind of gap the self-review pass exists to catch before a review board does.

questions.q: What honest alternative does this lesson's worked example name in step 1 for the Vantage Utilities case study, and why is it rejected?
options: Building a dedicated authenticated API, rejected because it's too slow to build
Letting the portal query Salesforce directly with a shared service-account token passed to the browser, rejected because a browser-exposed token can be read by anyone using developer tools
Using Change Data Capture instead of a REST API, rejected because CDC doesn't exist
No honest alternative is ever named for this case study
questions.explain: The worked example names the faster-to-build alternative of a shared token passed to the browser, then honestly rejects it: a token accessible from the browser is exposed to anyone who opens developer tools, which is an unacceptable security tradeoff.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why can a design that looks finished in a polished slide deck still fail a self-review pass?
options: Polished visuals automatically mean the underlying design is also sound
Visual polish (a clean diagram, confident bullets) can hide an unresolved failure mode or a hand-waved security answer underneath, which only the self-review steps actually surface
Slide decks are not allowed in integration architecture reviews
A design can never look finished unless it has already passed review
questions.explain: Looking finished is a presentation quality; being ready means the self-review steps found no unresolved gaps. A clean slide can disguise a hand-waved answer sitting underneath it, which is exactly what the self-review pass is meant to catch before a reviewer does.
